# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–17 (Complete – Updated 129)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Spring of fifth year** (Chapter 17 opening). Winter 1815-16 now passed. Waterloo campaign: 16 June 1815 morning—regiment receives marching orders and departs; afternoon/evening—cannonading; by 10 PM—Belgian hussar Regulus arrives in Brussels with tales of disaster; by dawn 17 June—wounded return in carts; afternoon 17 June—news of victory spreads; 18 June (Sunday)—religious services held. **Critical event (26 March 1816)**: Rebecca delivers son and heir to Rawdon. **Spring 1816**: Pitt marries Lady Jane at Brighton (arranged hastily by Miss Crawley after learning of Rebecca's pregnancy); they move into Miss Crawley's house. Lady Southdown assumes control of household. Miss Crawley dies (implied spring/early summer 1816). George Osborne's letter (written 16 June before dawn) delivered to his father approximately three weeks after 18 June—early July 1815. **Late autumn 1815**: Mr. Osborne announces trip abroad to Belgium; church incident with George's monument; subsequent meeting with Colonel Dobbin in Brussels.
- **Locations**: London (Russell Square, Thames Street, Slaughters' hotel, Gray's Inn Square, Hulker and Bullock bankers), Brussels, Belgium, Waterloo battlefield, Brighton, Southampton, Paris, Fenmere (hill farms), Salwick, various other towns.

## Main Characters

**Captain William Dobbin (now Colonel)**
- **Promoted to Major, then Colonel** in consequence of second Major's death on field at Waterloo. Greatly respected in regiment as best officer and cleverest man. Young Tom Stubble praised his modesty, kindness, and coolness in field. Before departure to campaign, came to Jos's quarters at dawn, instructed Jos to remain in Brussels and watch over Amelia. Secret, unrequited adoration of Amelia. **Late autumn 1815**: Still in Brussels with recovering regiment. **Critical Action - Confrontation with Mr. Osborne**: Encountered Mr. Osborne (George's father) in the street in Brussels; rode alongside him on horseback through town without speaking until reaching Mr. Osborne's hotel (formerly occupied by Crawleys). Followed Osborne to his apartments. **Presented Case for Reconciliation**: Pleaded with Osborne to forgive Amelia and unborn child; asked whether Osborne would visit "parent's offence upon the child's head" or forgive child for George's sake. **Result**: Osborne refused entirely, swearing never to recognize Amelia as his son's wife and to maintain position to last day of life. **Dobbin's Assessment**: Recognized hope was gone; realized Amelia's thoughts were not present due to catastrophic grief; understood she was stupefied under sorrow's pressure. **Dobbin's Role in Amelia's Recovery**: It was Dobbin who brought Amelia back to England to her mother's house when Mrs. O'Dowd received peremptory summons from her Colonel and was forced to quit patient. **Godfather to Amelia's child**: William became godfather of Amelia's infant; exerted ingenuity in purchasing cups, spoons, pap-boats, and corals for the little Christian. Amelia's laugh of triumph as she watched him holding the infant was gratifying.

**George Osborne**
- **DEAD at Waterloo (16 June 1815, though monument inscription states 18 June)** — discrepancy noted. Married Amelia late April without father's consent; disinherited (determination "final and irrevocable"). Received £2,000 in 4 percent annuities and £100/year widow's allowance for Amelia. At Brussels, carried on "desperate flirtation" with Rebecca; sent letter and bouquet to Rebecca after campaign began. Departed morning 16 June with regiment. **Written final letter before daybreak 16 June** to his father (not sent until July via Dobbin's officer) expressing: farewell on eve of great battle; solemn imploration to father to provide for Amelia and possible child; contrition for irregularities and extravagance; thanks; promise to act worthily. Letter sealed with sham coat of arms and "Pax in bello" motto. **The seal itself was robbed from George's dead body on field of battle**. **Monument Erected**: Elaborate monument erected in church with Osborne arms emblazoned. Inscription reads: "Sacred to the memory of George Osborne, Junior, Esq., late a Captain in his Majesty's --th regiment of foot, who fell on the 18th of June, 1815, aged 28 years, while fighting for his king and country in the glorious victory of Waterloo. Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori." Monument depicts Britannia weeping over urn, broken sword, couchant lion.

**Amelia Osborne**
- After George's departure: invalided; silent and haggard by windows watching bayonets march away. During cannonading: Mrs. O'Dowd spent five hours by her side. Upon hearing of victory: raved in hysteric insanity. Upon confirmation both George and Dobbin were safe: fell on Mrs. O'Dowd's neck in rapture, prayed gratefully. By 18 June: refreshed in health and spirits. **Currently** (late autumn 1815): **Widow and Mother**—George killed at Waterloo. **Delivered infant** (godchild to Colonel Dobbin). Status: receives £100/year widow's allowance; holds £2,000 in 4 percent annuities from George's estate. **Health and Mental State (Late Autumn 1815)**: "Very bad" condition reported; "out of her mind like for six weeks or more" per soldier's account. Life and reason "shaken by the blow which has fallen on her"; "very doubtful whether she will rally." However, recovery underway by time Dobbin brings her to England to her mother's house. Amelia's laugh of triumph as she watched Dobbin holding infant indicates improving spirits. Thoughts absorbed in grief; good and evil indifferent to her at lowest point.

**Captain Rawdon Crawley (now Lieutenant-Colonel)**
- **Married to Rebecca**. Made last dispositions for Rebecca's benefit before campaign. Rode by General's side. His gallantry mentioned in Gazette; promoted to Lieutenant-Colonel; awarded C.B. **Currently in Paris** with Rebecca, in track of conquering army. **By 26 March 1816**: Father of son and heir (announced in Galignani's Journal). Writes letters to Miss Crawley (written by Rebecca, attributed to Rawdon) from Paris, entertaining her with accounts of travels and sending war relics.

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley)**
- Post-departure activities in Brussels: secured financial independence through horse sales to Jos at prodigious price, sale of Rawdon's effects, stitched away trinkets, bills, bank-notes. **Currently in Paris** with Rawdon, flourishing in polite life among gayest conquerors. **Accommodates herself to fashionable life** as if ancestors were people of fashion for centuries past; from her wit, talent, and energy, merits place of honour in Vanity Fair. **By 26 March 1816**: Delivered son and heir. Writes all letters to Miss Crawley (attributed to Rawdon), sends war relics. **Miss Crawley's Fury**: Rebecca made use of Miss Crawley's name to gain entree into Parisian society. When Miss Crawley discovered this audacity, her fury was "beyond bounds." Too agitated to compose French reply, Miss Crawley dictated furious answer to Briggs in English, repudiating Rebecca altogether and warning public to beware of her as "most artful and dangerous person." However, Duchess of X (Parisian correspondent) did not understand English and reported to Rebecca that Miss Crawley sent "charming letter" with "benevolent things," causing Rebecca to hope spinster would relent.

**Jos Sedley**
- **Fled Brussels** 16 June toward Ghent road on horseback with Isidor, abandoning Amelia and company. Mrs. O'Dowd made scornful remarks upon his flight. **Current status (late autumn 1815)**: Widow Amelia's available source of financial aid, though his willingness uncertain.

**Miss Crawley (at Brighton, then with Pitt)**
- Worth approximately **seventy thousand pounds**. **DRAMATIC REVERSAL - Forced Marriage of Pitt and Lady Jane**: Upon learning of Rebecca's pregnancy and Rawdon's son (26 March 1816), Miss Crawley's rage reached its height. She immediately summoned Pitt and Lady Southdown and requested immediate celebration of pending marriage between Pitt and Lady Jane. Announced intention to allow young couple £1,000/year during her lifetime; bulk of property to settle upon Pitt and Lady Jane upon her death. Mr. Waxy (solicitor) came to ratify deeds. Marriage celebrated with Bishop. **After Marriage**: Pitt and Lady Jane moved into Miss Crawley's house. Her affection for Lady Jane had grown so strong she could not part with her favourite. **DOMINATED BY LADY SOUTHDOWN**: Lady Southdown from neighbouring house reigned over entire family—Pitt, Lady Jane, Miss Crawley, Briggs, Bowls, Firkin. Pitilessly dosed them with tracts and medicine; dismissed Creamer; installed Rodgers; stripped Miss Crawley of even semblance of authority. Miss Crawley grew so timid she ceased bullying Briggs and clung to Lady Jane. **DEATH**: Implied to have died spring/early summer 1816 during Lady Southdown's domination. Lady Jane supported her kindly in final days.

**Mr. Pitt Crawley (Bar of England)**
- **Married Lady Jane** (spring 1816, hastily arranged by Miss Crawley). **Now living in Miss Crawley's house** with wife. Miss Crawley allows them £1,000/year during her lifetime; bulk of her property settled upon them upon her death. **Greatly annoyed by humours** of his aunt on one side and mother-in-law Lady Southdown on the other. Lady Southdown reigns over entire household; Pitt conceived himself "most injured character." Diplomatic strategy fully succeeded—he is Miss Crawley's favoured nephew.

**Lady Jane Sheepshanks/Crawley**
- **Married Pitt Crawley** (spring 1816). **Living in Miss Crawley's house** with Miss Crawley and Pitt. Receives £1,000/year during Miss Crawley's lifetime (shared with Pitt); bulk of Miss Crawley's property settles upon her upon Miss Crawley's death. Remains kind and artless; Miss Crawley clung to her as favourite; presumed to have supported her kindly in final days.

**Mr. Osborne (Elder)**
- George's father in Russell Square, London. Upon learning George died at Waterloo (through George's letter), placed entire household in mourning—ordered elder daughter to place all females in mourning, male servants in deep black. Cancelled all parties and entertainments. Made no communication to future son-in-law Mr. Bullock (whose marriage to Osborne's daughter had been fixed); Mr. Bullock's appearance prevented pressing ceremony forward. Remained constantly in study; house front closed. Received George's letter three weeks after 18 June; trembled reading it, realizing his son was "still beloved and unforgiven." **Late Autumn 1815**: Announced trip abroad to Belgium. **In Brussels**: Visited hotel garden; sought out soldiers from --th regiment; paid guinea to wounded convalescent to bring Sergeant to Hotel du Parc (formerly Crawley lodgings). **Confrontation with Dobbin**: Encountered Colonel Dobbin; followed to his apartments at Hotel du Parc (George's former rooms). Dobbin pleaded for Osborne to forgive Amelia and unborn child. **Osborne's Response**: Broke out into rhapsody of self-praise and imprecations, excusing himself to conscience, exaggerating George's undutifulness. Insisted George died without confessing wrong; should take consequences. Swore never to speak to Amelia or recognize her as his son's wife. Stated he was "a man of his word" and would "stick to to the last day of my life." **Result**: Complete refusal of reconciliation. Soldiers received guineas from "proud purse of mourning old father" and feasted on his generosity.

**Other Characters**
- **Mrs. O'Dowd**: Spent five hours by Amelia's side during cannonading. Distinguished herself greatly at Waterloo; Major O'Dowd became Colonel and Companion of the Bath. Received peremptory summons from her Colonel in late autumn 1815, forcing her to quit patient Amelia.
- **Sir William Dobbin (Alderman)**: Called upon Mr. Osborne senior in Russell Square approximately three weeks after 18 June with pale, agitated face. Delivered George's sealed letter.
- **Osborne's Sisters (Maria and others)**: At church when monument agitated their nerves so much Miss Maria was compelled to leave. Clothed in deep black, sobbing. Wondered whether father would forgive Mrs. George. Conversed about possibility of reconciliation. Anxious regarding recognition of Amelia as family daughter. Had pretty accurate news of Amelia from Lady Dobbin and her daughters.
- **Tom Stubble, Pauline, Isidor, Towzer, Sergeant of Captain's Company, James Crawley (Jim)**: Status continued from previous summary.

## Critical Facts and Status
- **George's Monument and Inscription Discrepancy**: Monument inscription states George fell 18 June 1815, aged 28 years. However, established record shows George died 16 June 1815.
- **Waterloo Campaign Result**: George Osborne killed in action. Amelia widowed with £100/year allowance and £2,000 in annuities. Rawdon promoted to Lieutenant-Colonel, awarded C.B.
- **Amelia's Condition and Recovery**: Deeply traumatized; "out of her mind" for six weeks; life and reason shaken; doubtful recovery. However, brought to England by Dobbin to her mother's house when Mrs. O'Dowd recalled. Mother caring for her and infant. Recovering by late autumn 1815; showing signs of improved spirits.
- **Dobbin's Godparenthood**: William Dobbin godfather to Amelia's child; purchasing christening gifts. Brings joy to Amelia.
- **Mr. Osborne's Refusal of Reconciliation**: Categorically refused to recognize Amelia or support child. Maintained absolute position despite Dobbin's plea. Will not visit "parent's offence upon the child's head."
- **Miss Crawley's Property Secured for Pitt**: Successfully settled approximately seventy thousand pounds away from Rawdon and Rebecca through forced marriage of Pitt and Lady Jane to herself.
- **Rebecca's Audacity and Consequences**: Made unauthorized use of Miss Crawley's name in Paris society. Discovered and repudiated furiously by Miss Crawley, who warned public against her.
